title: Leak-safe validation: split by report-text hash
description:
Some reports are byte-identical across studies (a template read for an unremarkable knee), so every study in such a group gets the SAME derived target vector. Splitting a group across the divide scores the model on a target whose source it trained on.

Assign studies by a hash of the report text so duplicate groups stay whole. Hold out one fifth, fixed rather than rotated.

TWO REFERENCES, TWO MEANINGS: the holdout measures agreement with derived targets and has the numbers to select epoch and recipe. The annotation check measures agreement with a radiologist - what the competition scores - but only annotated studies inside the holdout may be used, and there are too few, so it is REPORTED and never allowed to arbitrate. Annotated studies stay in training at elevated weight, which is exactly why the check must exclude them.
notes:
CONFIRMED ON OUR DATA (probe v2, train.csv, 4407 studies): 4276 distinct reports, so 177 studies sit in a duplicate group. Group sizes: 27 pairs, 10 triples, one of 4, four of 5, one of 6, one of 12, one of 14, one of 37.

The largest group (37 studies) is a Turkish all-normal template: 'Diz eklemi ici sivi miktari normal. Capraz ve yan baglar normal...'. Next are Spanish templates at 14 and 12.

So the leak is real but bounded - 4% of studies. Splitting by report hash costs nothing and removes it; the 37-group alone would otherwise straddle the divide.
EMPIRICAL SUPPORT FOR 'THE ANNOTATION CHECK MUST NOT ARBITRATE' (2026-08-10, from the 20 published members):

Members differing ONLY by fold and seed - same architecture, same data, same recipe - report annotation-check scores from 0.7356 to 0.9164. That is a 0.18 spread on a metric that is supposed to measure the same thing, and it matches the Hanley-McNeil prediction (SE ~0.09 at A~0.8 with single-digit positives) almost exactly.

Their holdout scores over the same 20 members span only 0.8279 to 0.8600 - a 0.03 spread, six times tighter.

There is also structure, not just noise: every fold-2 member has a HIGH holdout (0.857-0.860) and a LOW annot (0.736-0.795). The annotated studies are distributed unevenly across folds, so which fold a member held out changes what its annotation check even measures.

So: select on the holdout, report the annotation check, and never let a 0.18-wide instrument arbitrate a 0.01 decision.

title: Slice ordering from geometry, never from file name
description:
Order each series by k = p.n where n = r_x cross r_y from ImageOrientationPatient and p = ImagePositionPatient. InstanceNumber is the fallback where geometry tags are missing (it tracks k up to sign, but interleaved/multi-echo acquisitions number out of spatial order and it is not signed in patient coordinates).

WHY: file names are SOP Instance UIDs - unique, not ordered. Sorting by them is reported at rho ~ 0.01 against physical position, and it fails SILENTLY: three-channel adjacent slices become three unrelated cross-sections, the middle of the stack becomes a random subset, and laterality reversal becomes a no-op.

PROVES: compute Spearman rho between filename order and geometric k on a sample of our series. Expect ~0.
notes:
CONFIRMED ON OUR DATA (probe v2, one 186-slice Philips series): Spearman rho(filename order, geometric k) = -0.0106. Filename order carries no anatomical information whatsoever.

Geometry tags are present on every slice of the sample: ImagePositionPatient 186/186, ImageOrientationPatient 186/186. So the exact ordering is available and the InstanceNumber fallback may be rarely needed - measure the tag-presence rate corpus-wide before relying on that.

k spans -68.6 .. 97.9 mm over the stack.

title: Series -> slot routing, with Fluid_Sensitive/Fat_Suppression recovered from the header
description:
Six slots: SAG_FLUID_FS, COR_FLUID_FS, AX_FLUID_FS, SAG_FLUID_NOFS, COR_T1, SAG_T1, plus a per-slot presence mask (a study rarely has all six).

MECHANISM: the shipped Fluid_Sensitive/Fat_Suppression columns are reported to agree on every training row, i.e. they carry ONE axis where the names claim two. Recover both from the header: weighting from TR/TE (T1: TR<~800; T2: TR>~800 and TE>~60; PD: TR>~800 and TE<~60), settled by ScanningSequence first because gradient echo breaks the TR rule; fat suppression from SeriesDescription/SequenceName/ScanOptions, falling back to TR/TE.

PROVES: on OUR copy of train_series.csv, measure the agreement rate between the two shipped columns. If it is 100%, the degeneracy is confirmed and recovery is mandatory, not optional.
notes:
CONFIRMED ON OUR DATA (probe v2, train_series.csv, 24371 rows): Fluid_Sensitive == Fat_Suppression on 1.000000 of rows. The crosstab is a clean diagonal - 10361 at (0,0), 14010 at (1,1), zero off-diagonal.

The two columns carry ONE axis, not two. Recovering both from the header (TR/TE/ScanningSequence for weighting, SeriesDescription/ScanOptions for fat-sat) is therefore mandatory, not an optimisation.

Corroborated by the sample series: SeriesDescription 'AX PD FS MPR L' with TR 1100 / TE 23 - TR>800 and TE<60 reads PD by the rule, and ScanOptions 'FS' gives the suppression independently. The rule reproduces the description.

Planes: Sagittal 9864, Coronal 8609, Axial 5898. Series per study mean 5.53, max 14 - so the six-slot scheme has real material to route.

title: Graft: inference-only kernel from pilkwang's mounted weights -> LB floor
description:
Mount pilkwang/rsna-knee-weights + pilkwang/rsna-knee-llm-labels + metaresearch/dinov2/PyTorch/small/1, run inference over the mounted test set, submit.

WHY: needs no local data and no training, and turns the field's public plateau (~0.899) into a measured number on OUR submission path. Same move as the biohub pilkwang graft.

HONESTY: the score is his result, not ours. Record it in comp/SUBMISSIONS.md as a graft; it must never appear in a README as our number, and it is a floor to build past, never an end state.
notes:
GRAFT, PHASE A IN PROGRESS (2026-08-10).

The weights manifest is fully self-describing: 20 members = 5 folds x 4 seeds, ALL one config (336px, 12 slices, group 3, crop 130mm, dinov2-small, cls_mean pool, prior false, unfreeze_last 6). One pixel_group, so a single decode serves all twenty. Their own numbers: holdout mean 0.8398 (min 0.8279, max 0.8600), annot mean 0.8375 (min 0.7356, max 0.9164).

Split into two phases because they have different prerequisites:
- PHASE A (no pixels needed): port the architecture and prove it faithful against the manifest's stored fingerprints. Done in kneemri/{model,slot_head,members}.py; comp/kernels/kneemri-graft-verify is the oracle.
- PHASE B (needs pixels): the data layer - slot routing, geometric ordering, laterality, crop/resample, decode-once cache. That is the bulk of the public notebook and wants local data, because debugging it one kernel push at a time is the slow way to do it.

LICENCE: both pilkwang datasets are CC0-1.0. The competition's own external-data clause is still unread (knee-0s6) - so NO SUBMISSION until that is settled.
PHASE A COMPLETE (2026-08-10): the architecture port is PROVEN faithful.

comp/kernels/kneemri-graft-verify v6: 20/20 members loaded and reproduced their stored fingerprints. Worst max|diff| = 4.65e-06 against a 2e-3 tolerance - a 430x margin, and squarely in the ~1e-5 GPU-numeric-noise band the tolerance was set between. Our StudyModel computes the same function these weights were fitted to; any error in pooling, ImageNet normalisation, resize or head would have moved it by order one.

Four kernel pushes were spent on mount/packaging shape, all cheap (pushes unlimited, no submission spent):
  v1-v3: mounts nest by kind (/kaggle/input/{competitions,datasets,models}/...) and a --dir-mode zip upload is expanded WITHOUT its wrapping directory, so kneemri_src/ never exists.
  v4: jaxtyping absent from Kaggle's image (see knee-61q note).
  v5: published checkpoints wrap weights under 'model' beside epoch/holdout/annot/config/oof/fingerprint.

REMAINS FOR THE GRAFT: Phase B, the data layer (knee-64b, knee-7ve, knee-e5e, knee-b0c, knee-37l). No submission until knee-0s6's external-data clause is read.

title: Check licence + external-data rules before submitting any grafted weights
description:
pilkwang/rsna-knee-weights (12+ checkpoints, ~89MB each) and the public LLM label tables are attached to public notebooks, which normally makes them permitted external data. Research competitions can restrict this, and a leaderboard row is public.

Verify the dataset licences and the competition's external-data clause BEFORE the graft submission. Record the finding here.
notes: LICENCE HALF RESOLVED (2026-08-10): pilkwang/rsna-knee-weights and pilkwang/rsna-knee-llm-labels are both CC0-1.0 per the dataset metadata API - fully permissive, no attribution condition. REMAINING: the competition's own external-data clause, which needs the rules page (JS-rendered, WebFetch returns nothing). Note the metadata API nests everything under an 'info' key; reading the top level silently returns None for every field.

title: Settle submission mechanics: notebook-only vs CSV upload
description:
comp/ is designed around the sibling competition's 400 FAILED_PRECONDITION "only accepts Submissions from Notebooks". Unverified here - the overview page is JS-rendered and WebFetch returns nothing.

Read the rules/overview pages, and confirm from the probe run. If CSV upload works, most of build_kit/publish is optional for this competition and the plan simplifies.

title: Probe kernel: environment facts + passthrough submission
description:
Push a kernel that writes sample_submission.csv unchanged to /kaggle/working/submission.csv and prints: torch version, cuda.device_count(), device name/arch, whether pydicom/timm/pandas are preinstalled, the competition mount paths, free RAM, and the wall-clock to read one DICOM series off the mount.

WHY: submission-path risk is the only risk that does not shrink by waiting, and it needs no local data and no model. Kernel pushes are unlimited; only submissions are 5/day, so probe freely.

PROVES: a scoreable submission.csv exists and the path works end to end. Expected LB = 0.5000 exactly (mean of twelve AUCs at chance) - any other value means the file or the metric is not what we think.
notes:
v1 FAILED (KernelWorkerStatus.ERROR): assumed the mount at /kaggle/input/<competition-slug> and died on FileNotFoundError in the first function, before any other probe ran. The mount name is not guaranteed to equal the slug. v2 discovers it by globbing for sample_submission.csv and prints the whole /kaggle/input listing either way. Confirmed from v1 regardless: Kaggle image is python 3.12 with pandas present.
PROBE v2 COMPLETE (2026-08-10). Every number below is measured, not borrowed.

MOUNT: /kaggle/input/competitions/rsna-knee-abnormality-detection - NOT /kaggle/input/<slug>. This is what killed v1 and it would have been baked into every kernel we wrote.

ACCELERATOR: machine_shape NvidiaTeslaT4 gives TWO Tesla T4, sm_75, 15.6 GB each. torch 2.10.0+cu128, arch_list includes sm_75 (so no P100 sm_60 problem while the metadata field is set). torch reports bf16_supported=True on sm_75 - treat as emulated, not native; keep inference fp16.

HOST: 4 CPUs only, 32.9 GB RAM (31.7 available). The 4-CPU count is the real constraint on any decode-heavy pipeline, and the cache budget must be sized against ~31.7 GB with train+test resident together.

LIBRARIES PRESENT OFFLINE: pydicom 3.0.2, timm 1.0.26, transformers 5.0.0, polars 1.35.2, cv2 4.13.0, SimpleITK 2.5.5, nibabel 5.4.2, einops 0.8.2, sklearn 1.6.1, scipy 1.16.3, PIL 11.3.0. ABSENT: monai, zarr. So the kit needs almost no wheels - unlike the sibling competition, which shipped six.

READ COST: 186 slices in 2.31 s = 12 ms/slice off the mount.
ADDENDUM - THE PROBE'S OWN BLIND SPOT (2026-08-10): it asked which libraries the PIPELINE needs (pydicom, timm, transformers, cv2, SimpleITK, sklearn, scipy, polars - all present) and never asked which ones OUR OWN SOURCE imports. jaxtyping is absent from Kaggle's image and kneemri/model.py imports it at module top, so the kit does need wheels (jaxtyping + wadler_lindig) after the earlier 'may need none' claim. Probe what you import, not only what you plan to use.
close_reason: Probe v2 complete; mount path, accelerator, offline library set, host limits and read cost all measured and recorded.

title: Verify the corpus facts the plan is built on
description:
Every number in this issue set came from a public notebook, not from our data. Once the download lands, verify on OUR copy and record the answers here: (1) do Fluid_Sensitive and Fat_Suppression agree on every row; (2) Spearman rho of filename order vs geometric k; (3) FOV distribution (Rows * PixelSpacing) median and range; (4) Laterality absence rate and vendor concentration; (5) per-label positive rate among annotated studies; (6) how many studies carry annotations vs reports only; (7) report language distribution; (8) byte-identical report duplicate-group sizes.

A borrowed constant that survives our own measurement is a finding; one that does not is a bug we would otherwise have inherited.
notes:
PARTIALLY ANSWERED WITHOUT THE DOWNLOAD (probe v2 reads train.csv and train_series.csv inside the kernel):

(1) Fluid_Sensitive vs Fat_Suppression agreement: 1.000000 over 24371 rows. Degenerate, confirmed. -> knee-64b
(2) Spearman rho filename vs geometric k: -0.0106 on a 186-slice sample series. -> knee-7ve
(3) FOV: 180.1 mm on the sample series (640 rows x 0.2815 mm). ONE series only - the corpus-wide distribution still needs the download before the crop extent is chosen.
(4) Laterality absence rate: NOT YET - the sample series carries Laterality 'L'. Needs a corpus sweep.
(5) Per-label prevalence: measured on all 58 annotated studies. -> knee-6xm
(6) Annotated vs report-only: 58 annotated / 4407 with reports. -> knee-6xm
(7) Report language distribution: NOT YET, but Turkish and Spanish both appear in the largest duplicate groups.
(8) Duplicate report groups: 4276 distinct over 4407; largest 37. -> knee-92z

REMAINING (need pixels): 3 corpus-wide, 4, 7.
DATA LANDED (2026-08-10): D:/data/volumetric/mri/raw/rsna_knee_abnormality/, 570 GB over 819,640 files, verified against the archive manifest.

Reconciles: 4407 train_series study dirs == train.csv rows; 3 test_series study dirs; train_series.csv (24371, 5); train.csv (4407, 14). core.paths.DataRoot.from_config(paths.yaml).raw() resolves and a DICOM reads through it.

EXTRACTION, measured: single-threaded unzip ran at 130 MB/s using 0.79 of ONE core out of 32, with disk queue length 0.00 - inflate-bound, NVMe idle. 16 parallel workers over contiguous central-directory slices hit 1040 MB/s peak / 598 MB/s average including the resume scan: 8x. The drives are rated 7-14 GB/s but those are sequential large-block figures; at 819,640 files averaging 695 KB the cost is DEFLATE plus per-file create/scan/close, not bandwidth.

TWO OBSERVATIONS FROM THE FIRST SAMPLE SERIES, both confirming audit predictions:
- Laterality was PRESENT BUT EMPTY (Type 2C). Recovery from patient-coordinate sign is needed, not optional (knee-e5e).
- 'DP SPIR CS_SAG' with TR 4244 / TE 22: the TR/TE rule reads PD and SPIR reads fat-suppressed, reproducing the description. 'DP' is French for proton density - the multilingual corpus reaches the headers too, not only the reports.

title: Treat the rare findings as the expensive ones
description:
Every label costs the same 1/12 of the score. A label left at chance contributes 0.5 instead of ~M, forfeiting (M-0.5)/12 however well the other eleven do - at M=0.85 that is 0.029, larger than most modelling gains.

So rare findings deserve MORE attention than common ones, because a rare finding is where a model most easily ends up at chance. Track per-label AUC from the first run and treat the worst label as the work item, not the mean.

Prevalence drift is survivable (AUC is in expectation invariant to positive rate, and the competition does not guarantee matched prevalence across train/public/final); thresholds are not.

title: Encoder adaptation: unfreeze the last blocks, two learning rates
description:
Adapt rather than freeze. Two restraints: only the last N transformer blocks move (early blocks are generic edge/texture filters - there may not be enough supervision to improve them and there is certainly enough to damage them), and the encoder learns far more slowly than the head (the head is random and has everything to learn; the encoder starts from a good solution and only needs moving off it). Reference point: head 1e-3 vs backbone 8e-6, last 6 blocks.

WHY NOT FROZEN: a frozen SSL encoder caps every downstream axis at once - resolution, size, coverage, aggregation all change how much it looks, none change the vocabulary it looks WITH. That ceiling should bind here: the features come from natural images, where nothing resembles a torn meniscus on a PD sequence.

title: Per-diagnosis query attention over slots, with a masked softmax
description:
Each of the twelve diagnoses gets its own query attending over the (up to six) slot embeddings, with absent slots masked OUT of the softmax so it renormalises over what the study actually contains.

WHY: mean-pooling the slots discards the reason the protocol has three planes - each finding is read on particular sequences, and a mean dilutes the one carrying the evidence with five that do not.

KEEP IT SMALL: the label is attached to the STUDY, so nothing in the supervision says which part carries the finding. Where the supervision is coarse, so is the head - a richer aggregator has no signal to learn from.
notes: IMPLEMENTED as kneemri/slot_head.py (SlotHead) during the Phase A port: per-diagnosis query, learned slot identity, masked softmax renormalising over present slots. Unit-tested including the property that masking a slot out equals never supplying it. Still to be trained by us - this is the replicated architecture, not our result.

title: Report-derived labels: adopt the public tables, then measure whether we can beat them
description:
Only a subset of training studies carry the twelve annotations; every training study carries a Report, and test.csv has NO Report column - so reports are training targets or sample weights, never an inference-time input.

Start by mounting the public LLM label tables (pilkwang, stevenleehans, lixin73-sol56) since every top notebook uses them. THEN attack them: labels are the ceiling on a weak-supervision task, and because the public tables are SHARED, improving them is edge nobody else has.

DIAGNOSTIC (needs no ground truth): the silence rate - for each (report, finding) pair, did anything match at all - tagged by language, says where the vocabulary is thin. Agreement-with-annotations cannot arbitrate: at A~0.8 with a handful of positives, the Hanley-McNeil SE is ~0.09, a 95% interval of +/-0.17, far wider than the differences being separated.
notes:
THE DEFINING FACT, measured (probe v2, train.csv 4407 x 14): all 4407 studies carry a Report, and only 58 carry all twelve annotations.

58 / 4407 = 1.3%. The competition is therefore a weak-supervision problem first and an imaging problem second: the labels for 98.7% of the training corpus have to be read out of free text, in nine languages, or not exist at all. This is why every top notebook mounts the same public LLM label tables, and why improving those tables is the highest-leverage un-shared axis available.

Prevalence among the 58 annotated studies: Effusion 0.603, Synovitis 0.466, Medial Meniscus 0.448, ACL 0.414, Lateral Meniscus 0.397, PF OA 0.362, Contusion 0.328, Fracture 0.310, Medial OA 0.259, Baker's 0.207, Lateral OA 0.190, MCL 0.155.

Read that as counts, not rates: MCL has NINE positives, Lateral OA eleven, Baker's twelve. Any model-selection decision made on the annotation check is being made on single-digit positive counts - which is exactly the Hanley-McNeil argument for why the holdout, not the annotation check, must arbitrate.

title: Decode-once pixel cache under a memory budget
description:
Decode slot images once into a uint8 in-memory cache; bytes = studies * slots * slices * P^2. Training draws one group of consecutive slices per step (doubles as augmentation along the stack); inference averages over groups.

WHY: a study is ~150 files and the pipeline is read-bound, not arithmetic-bound. Affordable once, not once per epoch.

CONSTRAINT: the cache grows with the SQUARE of resolution and only linearly with slices, so slice coverage is the cheap axis and resolution the expensive one. Budget a fraction of free memory (not all of it) and size TRAIN + TEST caches together, since both are resident at once - overshooting ends the run rather than slowing it.

title: Physical-scale crop + resample (mm/pixel is the design variable)
description:
Crop to a constant physical extent L and resample to P pixels, so effective pitch = L/P mm/pixel.

MECHANISM: a feature of width d survives only if pitch <= d/2 (Nyquist on the resampling grid). A meniscal tear is 1-3mm, so 1mm needs <= 0.5 mm/px. At L=130mm: P=224 gives 0.580 (fails), P=336 gives 0.387 (clears). The crop must be SMALLER than the smallest field of view or it silently does nothing.

PROVES: measure the acquired FOV distribution (Rows * PixelSpacing) over our training series. The claim to check is median ~160mm, range 70-320, and that 130mm sits below the FOV of ~99.6% of series. Pick L from OUR measurement, not from the quoted one.

title: Laterality normalisation, including recovery when the tag is absent
description:
Five of twelve targets are side-defined (two menisci, medial/lateral OA, MCL). Normalise: flip the last axis for coronal/axial (medial-lateral is in-plane); REVERSE THE SLICE ORDER for sagittal (medial-lateral is the slice axis).

Laterality is Type 2C and reported absent on half the studies, by whole vendors. Recover from patient coordinates: image centre c = p + r*ds*Nc/2 + d*dr*Nr/2; +x points to the patient's left, so sign(c_x) gives the side. Use the CENTRE, not p (a corner half a FOV away can flip the sign near the midline). Leave a study unresolved inside a ~20mm dead band rather than guessing.

PROVES: on our data, measure the Laterality-tag absence rate and its per-vendor concentration; check the recovered side against the tag where both exist.

title: comp/SUBMISSIONS.md: method-tuple naming + coverage grid
description:
Mirror the biohub convention: kernels named for the method tuple from a closed vocabulary, one subdir per method, and a coverage grid recording what has been tried vs what has not. The slug says which method it is; a new version of one slug is that same method retrained.

WHY: without it, submissions become an unlabelled pile and the 5/day budget gets spent re-running things whose result is already known. It is also where a grafted score is recorded AS a graft.

title: Combine members by rank, not by probability
description:
The score is the unweighted mean of twelve per-label ROC AUCs, invariant under any strictly increasing map, so calibration and thresholds are worth exactly nothing.

Averaging raw probabilities lets the most confident model dominate; averaging RANKS combines the only information the metric reads. Applies to member ensembling and to TTA pooling (logit-averaging is a geometric mean of odds, probability-averaging an arithmetic mean of risk - they order studies differently).

title: Members carry their preprocessing; verify by fingerprint before use
description:
A trained member is only reproducible together with the reading that produced it: resolution, crop, slice-order rule, laterality rule, slot-fill predicate, and the stand-in for a slice that will not decode. NONE of those change a single tensor shape.

So a member fitted under one reading and run under another loads cleanly, runs, and returns a submission computed from the wrong image. Ship the reading WITH the member, and have each member answer a seeded question whose expected answer travels with it; a mismatch stops the run rather than being averaged into a submission.

Group members by the pixels they need so one decode serves every member sharing it.

title: Backbone ablation: DINOv2 vs medical-pretrained
description:
Every public notebook mounts metaresearch/dinov2/PyTorch/small/1. Alternatives are already packaged as Kaggle datasets: RadImageNet ResNet-50, MedicalNet ResNet-50 (3D), BiomedCLIP.

The field defaulted to DINOv2 with no visible evidence against domain-matched medical pretraining. Natural-image SSL may well win, but it is untested here, which makes this a cheap and uncrowded axis once a harness exists.

NOTE: no internet in kernels - a backbone must be a MOUNTED Kaggle model, never a download.

title: Graded targets + confidence as sample weights
description:
Reports are graded, annotations are thresholded: "small joint effusion" can sit against a NEGATIVE annotation because the annotator marked only significant ones. So "term present => positive" is wrong by construction; grade the mention (trace / unqualified / marked) instead - and it costs nothing, because the metric reads only order.

Carry a per-finding confidence as a sample weight so a report that never mentions synovitis pulls weakly on that head rather than asserting a negative. Weight the image-annotated studies above every derived row - they are the only labels read from the images.

title: Decide whether to target the Efficiency Prize
description:
There is a separate Efficiency Prize leaderboard (Holbrook's notebook, 106 votes). Decide deliberately whether to target it, because it changes inference-cost choices (resolution, member count, TTA breadth) that are otherwise free.

Defaulting into it by accident is the failure mode: optimising cost without the prize, or eating cost that disqualifies us from it.
